title: electroreduction to C2 fuels
abstract: Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) to obtain C2/multi-carbon fuels is an appealing technology to reduce carbon emission and store intermittent renewable electricity. The C–C coupling process, as the most critical step for generating C2/multi-carbon fuels, strongly depends on the concentration of ∗CO intermediates around the active sites. In this work, we prepared porous copper nanospheres (P-Cu) that greatly improved the C–C coupling process by enriching ∗CO intermediates in the pore structure. The specific pore features of P-Cu were characterized in detail by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and nitrogen adsorption/desorption tests. Obviously, the P-Cu exhibits higher specific surface area and richer pore structure than the control sample compact copper nanosphere (C-Cu). The CO gas sensor and temperature programmed desorption (TPD) tests prove that the P-Cu has better CO adsorption and enrichment capacity than C-Cu due to the rich pore structure. As a result, P-Cu exhibited a high C2 selectivity with a Faradaic efficiency (FE C2 ) of 57.22% at −1.3 V ( vs . RHE), which is about 2.5-fold than the C-Cu (FE C2 of 22.71%). This work provides an effective strategy to improve the activity and selectivity of C2 products in CO 2 RR by optimizing the adsorption/enrichment property of intermediates. © 2021 Elsevier Ltd. Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) to obtain C2/multi-carbon fuels is an appealing technology to reduce carbon emission and store intermittent renewable electricity. The C–C
coupling process, as the most critical step for generating C2/multi-carbon fuels, strongly depends on the concentration of ∗CO intermediates around the active sites. In this work, we prepared porous copper nanospheres (P-Cu) that greatly improved the C–C coupling process by enriching ∗CO intermediates in the pore structure. The specific pore features of P-Cu were characterized in detail by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and nitrogen adsorption/desorption tests. Ob-
viously, the P-Cu exhibits higher specific surface area and richer pore structure than the control sample
compact copper nanosphere (C-Cu). The CO gas sensor and temperature programmed desorption (TPD)
tests prove that the P-Cu has better CO adsorption and enrichment capacity than C-Cu due to the rich
pore structure. As a result, P-Cu exhibited a high C2 selectivity with a Faradaic efficiency (FE C2 ) of 57.22% at −1.3 V ( vs . RHE), which is about 2.5-fold than the C-Cu (FE C2 of 22.71%). This work provides an effective strategy to improve the activity and selectivity of C2 products in CO 2 RR by optimizing the adsorption/enrichment property of intermediates.

. Introduction
Modern energy consumption and chemical industries highly de-
end on fossil resources. The burning of fossil fuels leads to mas-
ive emission of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), which is regarded as an mportance contributor to greenhouse effect [ 1 , 2 ]. The CO 2 elecrochemical reduction reaction (CRR) using renewable electricity is
egarded as a clean and feasible approach to solve the problem
f the raised concentration in atmospheric. Recently, CRR has re-
lized electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to C1 [3–7] ( e.g. , CO, CH 4 , nd HCOOH) and multi-carbon products [8–12] . Among these CRR
roducts, multi-carbon products ( e.g. , C 2 H 4 [13–15] , C 2 H 5 OH [16] , 2 H 6 ) attract more attention, owing to its higher energy density nd value than C1. To date, the Cu-based catalysts are the mostly
emonstrated catalysts for C2 formation in CRR [ 17 , 18 ]. However,
he poor selectivity and activity of C2 products of Cu-based cat-
lysts limit the practical applications of CRR. Thus, it is emerged

etermined by the morphology [ 4 , 19 , 20 ], size [21] , and surficial
tomic/electronic arrangement [22–24] . The facet exposure[ 25 , 26 ],
hich often affects the CRR performance, can be controlled via
uning morphology of Cu-based catalysts, such as Cu nano-cubes
27] , Cu octahedral [28] , and Cu nanowires [ 4 , 29 ] etc. Besides, in-
reasing the size of Cu nanoclusters could improve catalytic activ-
ty and selectivity toward C2 productions in CRR [21] . Moreover,
he surficial state of Cu-based materials can be modified by alien
pecies doping [3] , defect engineering [ 30 , 31 ], and lattice boundary
ngineering. These methods can effectively promote the CRR per-
ormance via tuning the C–C coupling state during reaction. How-
ver, it is ignored that the highly active catalysts are usually ac-
ompanied with the reconstruction, which could lead to the cat-
lyst deactivation [ 7 , 32–34 ]. Therefore, developing materials with
igh structure stability is arising as new type catalysts for CRR.
he porous Cu shows high structural stability during CRR with
igh catalytic performance. Intriguingly, the porous Cu-based ma-
erials possess defect-rich structure and extraordinary mass trans-

.1. Chemicals

Preparing porous and compact Cu 2 O electrodes are reduced to u via electroreduction in 0.1 M KHCO 3 solution at −1.3 V vs. RHE or 30 min.

rom a FEI Helios Nanolab 600 field emission electron micro-

. Conclusion
In summary, we prepared P-Cu via in-situ reduction method
n CRR system. The porous structures show high catalytic perfor-
ance than solid Cu sphere, including C –Cu and ball griding P-Cu.
he C2 selectivity of P-Cu is up to 57.22% at potential of −1.3 V s. RHE, which is ca. 2-fold and 1.5-fold of C –Cu and ball griding
-Cu, respectively. The P-Cu shows high structure stability and cat-
lytic activity during CRR. The high catalytic performance of P-Cu
an be assistant with the high surface area and spatial confine-
ent effect. Besides the highly intrinsic catalytic activity, the spa-
ial confinement effect can promote C–C couplings formation on
nner-surface of P-Cu, and thus highly enhance the C2 products.
ur work provides a direction for discussion and further research
n electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction performance of Cu-
ased electrodes.
